pleistocene.summary: The epoch of repeated glacial cycles, during which ice sheets advanced and retreated more than twenty times and the genus Homo spread across the globe.

homo-habilis.summary: The earliest widely accepted member of our genus, with a larger brain than the australopithecines and a firm association with stone tools.
homo-habilis.note: Whether habilis belongs in Homo at all is a long-running argument.

homo-erectus.summary: The first hominin with body proportions like ours, the first to leave Africa, and the longest-lived species of human by a wide margin — nearly two million years, roughly ten times our own run so far.

acheulean-handaxe.summary: A symmetrical teardrop tool made to essentially the same design across Africa, Europe and Asia for more than a million years — the longest unchanged technology in human history.

control-of-fire.summary: Cooking releases far more energy from food than chewing raw, and is widely argued to be what allowed brains to grow while guts shrank.
control-of-fire.note: Scattered evidence goes back 1.5 million years; habitual, controlled use is only firmly attested from around 400,000 years ago.

homo-heidelbergensis.summary: A widespread population generally taken to be the common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans and ourselves, though the naming is contested.

neanderthals.summary: Cold-adapted humans across Europe and western Asia with brains as large as ours, who buried their dead, made ochre pigment and glue, and cared for the injured. They interbred with our ancestors, and most people outside Africa carry a small percentage of their DNA.

homo-naledi.summary: A small-brained human found deep inside a South African cave system, alive at the same time as the first Homo sapiens.
homo-naledi.note: Claims that it deliberately buried its dead are disputed and would be remarkable for a brain a third the size of ours.

homo-sapiens.summary: Anatomically modern humans appear in Africa and subsequently disperse across every continent.
homo-sapiens.note: The Jebel Irhoud fossils push anatomically modern traits back to about 315 ka; fully modern morphology is usually placed nearer 200 ka.

denisovans.summary: A sister group to the Neanderthals spread across Asia, whose genes survive in present-day populations from Melanesia to Tibet, including a variant that makes high-altitude life possible.
denisovans.note: Known almost entirely from DNA rather than bones — a finger fragment, a few teeth and a jaw. A whole human population identified by genome first.

behavioural-modernity.summary: Engraved ochre, shell beads, pigment and long-distance exchange appear in Africa long before the European cave paintings — evidence of minds that dealt in symbols.
behavioural-modernity.note: Whether this was a sudden revolution or a slow accumulation is one of the central arguments in palaeoanthropology.

last-glacial-period.summary: The most recent ice age, when ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Eurasia and sea level fell by about 125 metres.

homo-floresiensis.summary: A metre-tall human on the Indonesian island of Flores, shrunk by island isolation and surviving until our own species arrived nearby.

out-of-africa.summary: A relatively small population left Africa and, within forty thousand years, occupied every continent except Antarctica.
out-of-africa.note: Earlier excursions reached the Levant by 190,000 years ago but left no descendants; this is the dispersal everyone outside Africa descends from.

toba-eruption.summary: A supervolcanic eruption in Sumatra, the largest of the Quaternary, followed by a volcanic winter of disputed severity.

aboriginal-australia.summary: Humans crossed Wallacea to reach Sahul, beginning the longest continuous cultural tradition known.

cave-art.summary: Painted animals and hand stencils in Sulawesi, Borneo and southern France, including what may be the oldest narrative scene yet found. The Sulawesi dates overturned the assumption that such art began in Europe.

neanderthal-extinction.summary: The last Neanderthal populations vanish a few thousand years after Homo sapiens reaches Europe, leaving us the only human species on Earth for the first time in millions of years.

dog-domestication.summary: The first domesticated animal, thousands of years before any plant or livestock, and the only one that arguably chose us as much as we chose it.
dog-domestication.note: Where and how many times wolves were domesticated is unsettled; the genetic and archaeological dates disagree.

last-glacial-maximum.summary: The peak of the last ice age, when continental ice sheets reached their greatest extent and Beringia linked Asia to the Americas.

peopling-of-americas.summary: Humans crossed from Siberia into a continent with no people in it, and reached the southern tip of South America within a few thousand years.
peopling-of-americas.note: The old Clovis-first model is dead. Footprints at White Sands may push arrival back to 23,000 years ago, and a coastal route is now favoured over an ice-free corridor, but the earliest dates remain disputed.

jomon-period.summary: Hunter-gatherers who made some of the oldest known pottery anywhere and sustained a settled way of life for ten thousand years without farming.
